The code for our research will be made available at https://github.com/ronitack/MEE.

Over the past 25 years, music and sound signals have become a popular subject of study in the information theory community, with applications spanning from media processing to cognitive science. This interest is largely due to the diverse nature of music, which makes it challenging to model. This paper contributes to this field by introducing a new measure of music complexity that combines two existing methods: recurrence plots and symbolic dynamics. This proposed measure is applied to "The Top 40 Music Database-2", a comprehensive collection of the top 40 Western music tracks from as early as 1959. Utilizing this approach, the temporal evolution of music complexity is tracked and analyzed, yielding contrasting outcomes for vocal (lyric) and instrumental components. The results obtained from modern Western music are then compared with previous findings from traditional Japanese traditional music.

A set of $N$ numbers, ranging from 0 to 1, is initially arranged in increasing order. At each of the infinite stages of a process, a new number, denoted as $U_{N+k}$, is randomly added to this sequence and all numbers are re-sorted. The behavior of certain statistics derived from the lengths of consecutive numbers and areas under curves formed by these numbers is analyzed as both $N$ and $k$ approach infinity.

Our research investigates the concept of computational play to uncover innovative methods for engaging with technology through play. We create interactive art and design frameworks that stimulate the development of systems capable of playing and facilitating play in novel ways. The case studies presented in this paper illustrate a balanced approach, combining artistic expression and technical innovation in the realm of computational play.

Reward learning is a fundamental component of reinforcement learning, yet it is notoriously difficult to learn due to the need to identify and label distinct regions of the reward space. In this paper, we introduce an efficient approach to learn cluster-based reward functions through human comparisons, via an optimization method that effectively utilizes human input by concentrating on time-sensitive, region-defined comparisons. Our method employs visual aids to guide humans to focus on specific reward spaces, thereby reducing the necessary number of comparisons. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our method, requiring fewer comparisons than baseline methods.

Every monad in the category of binary signed sets, known as Smyth domains, has a corresponding monad in the category of binary sets. We identify a fundamental requirement for this image monad to be a core-compact space monad. Additionally, we determine which monads can be transformed into such a monad via a corial adjunction.

By applying an external force, we can create vortex loops in a 2D perfect liquid.
These vortex structures aim for the minimum energy state and, in a supercooled liquid,
take the form of connected clusters of vortices with like spins adjacent to each other.
We experimentally and theoretically investigate the characteristics of these vortex
loop clusters, including their size, shape, orientation, speed, and the conditions
for their stability. Our study also involves the numerical simulation of loch and
crane version of the superfluid for comparison and in understanding of the effect
of the reduced viscosity.

A novel technique, Standardized Enhanced Inverse Likelihood Weighting (SEILW), has been developed to improve the accuracy of ensemble-enhanced weather forecasts generated using Neural Networks. By integrating the SEILW method, which relies on model output standard deviations and post-processing, with a neural network-derived forecast method, such as the FNN-EW method, a linear combination of weighted forecasts is achieved. This SEILW method can be applied to any type of post-processing or ensemble-enhanced forecast. In our study, a SEILW method is specifically tailored for the FNN-EW method, and this combination is evaluated in two geographical locations, Sydney and Houston, for their respective temperatures at 2 meters. Results indicate that SEILW yields a 6 to 10 percent enhancement in the correlation coefficient and a 6 to 10 percent improvement in the root mean square error compared to the FNN-EW method in our test cases.

LHC experiments have found that tau lepton width is smaller than predicted by theory, 
creating a significant discrepancy that persists despite a shift in the observed shortfall 
following recent updates to experimental data. This anomaly poses a significant test 
for new physics theories that enhance the tau without modifying other lepton properties. 
In this article, we will review the theoretical and experimental difficulties in 
measuring this accuracy, and discuss how generic new physics models can be developed 
to address this accuracy off the LHC grid.

A thorough investigation into the impact of terrain on atmospheric circulation patterns in a rotating, temperature-stratified fluid is presented. A series of experiments were conducted using a clear, rotating tank to observe how different tank shapes and fluid conditions affect wave dynamics. These experiments were paired with detailed 3D simulations using the Spectral Element method to analyze both stable and unstable flow regimes. When the tank has flat side walls, multiple waves form and move in the direction of the rotation. Introducing an obstacle in the tank disrupts this rotation and causes the waves to shift perpendicularly to the rotation axis. Introducing an obstacle in the tank also causes the onset of turbulence to occur at a lower rotation rate than in a flat-walled tank. In addition, introducing an obstacle in the tank also causes the rotation of the fluid to cause the fluid to form irregular patterns and irregular patterns and irregular patterns and irregular patterns

Reparametrizing the exponential measure, we establish a novel arrival process that serves as an efficient indicator for the presence of extreme events. The parameters of this arrival process can be directly linked to traditional extreme value theory parameters, and we show that it can be independently model and infer for each threshold utilized in the analysis. We develop a Bayesian approach that yields reliable estimates and credible intervals, and we test their consistency through extensive simulations. Ultimately, we apply our method to analyze storm surges in the Netherlands between 1675 and 2015, providing a range of estimates for future scenarios.

A common challenge in reinforcement learning is the issue of corruption resilience, especially when learning occurs in a changing world where some experiences are lost and others are added due to interference. Although online learning methods can theoretically achieve this, they often fail in offline learning due to the inability to react quickly to experience changes. Our study focuses on a more feasible scenario for offline learning where the rate of experience change remains within certain limits, allowing for the prior knowledge of the environment to guide policy selection. Under these conditions, we propose a new offline learning algorithm, $B\alpha U$LE, which is proven to have linear scalability in terms of changes within the environment. Our study shows that $B\alpha ULE$ has linear regret growth, making it significantly more efficient than previous methods with sublinear performance guarantees. Furthermore, our online extension of the algorithm, B$\alpha ULE^{\ast}$, exhibits a level of robustness in real-world tests, even in the presence of significant experience modifications.

One-dimensional heat equations with non-uniform boundary conditions are investigated, yielding a condition that ensures the capacity for immediate control. This condition, essentially a logarithmic convexity requirement similar to that of G. Da Prato's work but with a simplified expression, can be seen as analogous to an entropy condition in hydrodynamics, aligning with observations by H. Fuchs and S. Reichel. As a direct consequence, a control formula is developed that provides an estimate for the control norm based on the distance between the final temperature and the specified target temperature.

Identifying the origin of an input beyond its training distribution is crucial for both AI-driven decision-making systems and general machine learning applications. This paper explores six distinct types of out-of-distribution inputs, each with unique characteristics and inherent limitations in their detection methods. To improve EOID capabilities, the study introduces a framework for constructing diverse distributions that enables models to function effectively in various scenarios, including the ability to reason about the origin of an input. This framework is demonstrated through its application on a dataset simulating textual descriptions of images.

A nanoscale molecular engine, attached to a solid substrate, nanotube, and brownian bead, has been studied. Upon tunneling of inelastic electrons from the substrate to the molecule and back to a gate, the molecule gains vibrational energy and transfers it to the bead, doing mechanical work. This system can be visualized as a tunneling site, a molecular motor, and a viscous bath. It exhibits distinct time scales and non-Markovian characteristics. A detailed and non-Markovian stochastic framework has been developed to simulate this brownian engine and the electron-tunneling dynamics. This framework incorporates electron tunneling rates, molecular vibrations, and electron back-tunneling probabilities. It includes the back-reaction of the current on the molecular motor and the molecular motor's effect on the current. This non-Markovian framework was developed based on the quantum master equation and was validated by direct numerical simulations of the full Hamiltonian. It was found that the molecular engine exhibits optimal power output at specific operating conditions, and the model also captures electron tunneling fluctuations and non-linear tunneling effects.

Unilateral synchronization of two terminal tools can unidirectionally convert any input language of the tool pair to a term, resulting in the same output language as a unidirectional conversion. Unidirectional conversion from structured input to structured output is generally not unilateral convertible. Unidirectional conversion from structured input to structured output is not universally unilateral convertible. To address this limitation, we establish an alternative form of unilateral conversion known as unidirectional resynchronization, allowing modified tools to Unidirectionally resynchronize with each other. Furthermore, we unilateral convert several classes of unilateral tools, including tree-adjunctive homomorphisms, and we unilateral convert the tools from tree-adjunctive homomorphisms to monoid homomorphisms.

This research paper examines the concept of polynomial or power series composition, often referred to as hashtabli in Chinese, with the aim of providing an algorithm for achieving this. Notably, our findings show that this process can be completed in nearly linear time, even in the context of rings that do not possess the property of being an integral domain, as long as the time complexity for determining the inverse of a series remains constant. This algorithm is particularly useful in the field of free monoid enumeration, where it enables accelerated computation of certain enumerating series, as well as in other fields such as combinatorial analysis and symbolic computation.

The discovery of ultra-cool companions like T-dwarves has been a significant achievement in modern astronomy, but isolated objects of this type have remained elusive due to their faintness and the limited spectral coverage of high-resolution spectrographs. However, with the development of sophisticated analysis tools, researchers have been able to obtain accurate atmospheric parameters for these objects, including the atmospheric parameters of the isolated T-dwarf GJ 229Ab. By utilizing the line profile retrieval code APOLLO, which leverers a Bayesian approach, researchers have been able to obtain atmospheric parameters for T-dwarves, including those of GJ 229Ab. By comparing the results of this analysis with those of warmer M-dwarves and cooler Y-dwarves, researchers have been able to determine that GJ 229Ab has an effective temperature of 630±10 K, placing it at the boundary between M and Y types. This is in contrast to other analysis methods, which have yielded conflicting results regarding its classification. Moreover, the analysis also reveals that clouds play a significant role in the atmosphere of GJ 229Ab, which is consistent with other cool dwarves. This is significant because it suggests that certain previously unidentified absorption features may be attributed to cloud contributions rather than molecular bands. This is particularly relevant when considering that molecular models without clouds fail to accurately reproduce the observed spectra of many T-dwarves.

In this study, an investigation is conducted to uncover the characteristics of the $0^{--}$ state. The production mechanisms for this resonance are explored, specifically through $e^+e^-$ annihilation at both threshold and high energy. The $e^+e^- \gamma$ process is selected for further consideration, and relevant decay rates are also examined. The findings suggest that a detailed analysis of the $e^+e^- \gamma$ decay could be a valuable tool in understanding the properties of this $0^{--}$ state.

Our re-analysis of LHCb data has led to a more rigorous test of the Standard Model in the phase difference between different decays of the $B_s$ meson, with the calculated value of $\phi_s$ matching predicted models within confidence intervals. In addition, we have determined the half-life difference between $B_s$ meson decays, with the calculated value of $\Delta\Gamma_s$ also consistent with predictions from different Standard Model calculations. In contrast, this value is significantly divergent from the initial LHCb measurement, with the calculated value lying outside of its confidence intervals. In order to further investigate the differences, we have made predictions for future data collections and potential areas of study.

A mathematical model for predicting SARS-CoV-2 virus propagation on crowded buses during the pandemic has been developed. The study leverages well-mixed system theory to analyze the spread of the virus, examining how airborne viruses and asymptomatic infected individuals contribute to its spread. Utilizing data from Milan, a single, heavily used bus route, was used to illustrate the model's application. Key parameters were measured and estimated for this framework. The research found that the rate of virus spread is directly proportional to the rate of new passengers boarding the bus. The study identified two primary factors influencing virus propagation: the duration of the bus route and the level of ventilation. The model's findings have significant implications for public health policy and disease control measures on public transportation.

To gain insight into unique beta decay features, such as those seen in forbidden non-unique cases, it's crucial to have an accurate understanding of the characteristics of parent and daughter nuclei. This research applies the shell model to examine beta decays related to the 50 to 82 neutron shell closure, specifically focusing on the $^{133}$Te ($^{132}$Sn) to $^{133}$Sn ($^{132}$Sn) and $^{135}$Te to $^{135}$Xe ($^{134}$Xe) decays. By comparing the calculated log $ft$ values and L values of these forbidden beta decays with experimental data, two models, including the standard shell model and the generalized seniority model, are evaluated. Although the generalized seniority model is simpler and includes fewer components, it offers a useful initial approximation. However, for an accurate theoretical description, the standard shell model is necessary.

A Double-Ended Auction protects participants in a transaction by ensuring that
neither party obtains the item until both parties receive their intended outcomes.
A crucial application of this concept lies in token sales, where investors and
token holders engage in a transaction. However, current token sales often lack
authentication, rendering participants susceptible to deception. To rectify this
issue, we introduce a novel Double-Faced Authentication protocol, Verifiable VAT,
which not only guarantees participant authentication but also guarantees
authentication outcomes. Furthermore, our protocol is efficient in terms of space
and communication, requiring only a constant factor increase in both aspects to
achieve this. Our research showcases the effectiveness of our protocol through a
successful implementation in a real-world setting, yielding positive outcomes.

The bottom mesons in the HQET framework are investigated, utilizing the light-front quark model. Calculations of the masses, decay constants, and wave functions of these mesons, including the $B_s$, $B_s^*$, and B mesons, yield the following results. Additionally, we calculate the masses, decay constants, and wave functions of the bottom mesons, yielding the following results. Finally, we calculate the masses, decay constants, and wave functions of the bottom mesons, including the $B$, $B^*$, and other mesons, yielding the following results.

Gurvits and Katinis introduced the concept of a composition being in the minimal relation when given operators on a vector space with the same finite dimension. They demonstrated that this concept is inherent to the structure of the Truncated Path Category, which they applied to show the completeness of periodic functions on the circle under the metric of bounded variation and homogeneous norm. This paper expands upon their work by defining the relationship between paths having a minimal period and showing its applicability to nonexpansive curves, which leads to several new results regarding their properties.

A popular technique, Resilient Education for Linearization of Complex Systems, helps uncover essential linear approximations of complex, nonlinear patterns from data, specifically in applications like fluid dynamics. However, it struggles with large datasets and noisy conditions. A new method, LANDO, has been created to address these limitations by training an artificial intelligence model to predict linearizations of complex patterns. LANDO integrates this model with a modification of the technique, allowing it to analyze data resampling, dynamically learn patterns, and incorporate both artificial and measured data to fill gaps in nonlinear patterns. LANDO's performance has been tested on various flow scenarios, including the流动 structure of the Göttingen Diffuser and a direct numerical simulation of a diffuser flow, specifically the study of diffuser stalls. LANDO's results show it can accurately capture key frequencies and structures, even in datasets with data gaps, limited samples, and noise.

Complex systems in nature and human activities are characterized by their intricate and interconnected nature. Understanding and analyzing their inner workings and behaviors are challenging, but their underlying patterns and similarities can be captured and measured using various metrics. One such measure is based on the concept of fuzzy sets, which can be used to model and analyze complex systems by extracting relevant information and comparing their internal structures and behaviors. This paper presents a new application of fuzzy sets to analyze the movements of chess players at the beginning of a game, using data from the LinkedIn chess community and incorporating factors such as the color of the pieces, the position of the pieces, and the type of chess opening used. Our results show that the proposed measure can provide accurate and reliable assessments of the structures of the chess opening repertoires, comparable to those obtained through traditional combinatorial methods, and also reveal new insights into the dynamics of the chess community and the behavior of individual players.

We've developed a comprehensive, self-consistent approach to determine millisecond pulsar parameters using pale dwarf companions. Our method relies on independently determining the companion's mass through a self-consistent analysis of its light curve, which in turn allows for the direct calculation of the pulsar's spin period without relying on external assumptions. Additionally, we derived a new analytical expression for the white dwarf radius, incorporating all relevant apsidal effect parameters. This approach was applied to three pale dwarf systems with previously unknown pulsar spin periods, yielding precise measurements aligned with existing estimates. Our results also confirm that the spin-orbit alignment assumption holds for these systems, as indicated by the parameter $w$. These findings demonstrate that pale dwarf systems serve as valuable tools for determining millisecond pulsar parameters, offering an alternative to traditional timing methods.

A comprehensive theory has been developed to describe various forms of energy and motion conservation for equations of motion derived from higher-derivative Lagrangians. The novel frameworks for identifying nonlocal constants of motion and generalized energies have been created, which cover all possible orders of motion derivatives in their respective equations. The theory's conditions are formulated as requirements for specific derivatives of the motion, and it has been applied to motions with higher derivatives in Lagrangian form. The study also examines the energy behavior and stability of certain systems, such as Klein-Glasson and Dirac fields, and demonstrates how motion derivatives can affect their dynamics.

This work introduces a method for creating and retrieving 3D forms through a free-drawing technique in a virtual reality (VR) environment. By integrating this approach with specialized input devices, it becomes feasible to interact with a 3D space in an immersive manner, opening up possibilities for applications in drawing, design, and other related fields. To validate this concept, we developed a prototype app for the Oculus Rift and conducted a user study to assess its practicality. For storage and visualization purposes, the drawn objects are reconstructed as tetrahedral meshes, which are then stored in a database and can be matched against query data. Our results indicate that free-drawing is a viable approach for 3D creation and highlight its potential applications and uses.

HD80606b, a planet with a highly eccentric orbit, undergoes dramatic changes in its host star's irradiation, experiencing a rapid and intense heating process that can trigger a variety of astrophysical phenomena. Due to its irregular 111-day orbital period, accurately predicting the planet's periastron passage is essential for observing such events via the James Webb Space Telescope. This research aims to refine HD806006b's periastron time just-in-time for JWST's upcoming observations. By analyzing historical photometric and spectrometric data, and incorporating new observations from a simultaneous stellar occultation monitoring project utilizing a global network of telescopes, the study refines its periastron passage prediction, initially placing it at 12 years into JWST's operational cycle.

A key characteristic of black holes in general relativity is the presence of certain black hole types that are considered extremal. These types are characterized by the satisfaction of the generalized second law of thermodynamics only at its most basic level. By applying a type of Iyer-Wald formalism for black holes and various modifications to the Einstein-Seymour-Schutz-Scullion framework, new expressions for the thermodynamic properties of black holes are developed. These modifications yield novel insights into the thermodynamic properties of black holes and identify conditions under which they become extremal. These conditions are characterized by various aspects, including the satisfaction of thermal equilibrium, mass and angular momentum conservation, and specific relationships between these variables. The study also reveals that the specific heat of black holes is a measure of their stability, with regions where the heat takes on opposite signs indicating different types of stability. The work also identifies conditions under which the extremal properties of black holes can be derived, providing a deeper understanding of the thermodynamic properties of these objects.

The effectiveness of training engines is largely constrained by the inability to effectively utilize training data, particularly the starting and concluding frames. Recent research has revealed that initial frames have minimal impact on engine training outcomes, leading to a waste of valuable computational resources. A new framework, EpIFN, has been proposed to effectively utilize all frames in the training data, including initial frames. EpIFN's success relies on its ability to effectively utilize concluding frames through the development of a novel marker-based investigation push, incorporating both marker-assisted back-propagation and investigation push markers, as well as a marker-driven push investigation through analysis of concluding frames. Experimental results using public datasets have demonstrated that EpIFN outperforms existing engines in terms of accuracy, particularly for action classification through the Kenem5 dataset and the Actionbank dataset.

We've developed a framework for vibrant Poincaré symmetry, a concept that introduces novel features while retaining the core principles of conventional Poincaré symmetry. This new symmetry gives rise to novel mechanisms for particle and field creation, as well as a field representing a novel form of Poincaré gravity. The process involves solving the constraints generated by the symmetry's zero-mode, resulting in a novel mechanism where the gravity field acts as a generator driving the creation of other gravitational and particle modes. This mechanism provides a potential path for naturally generating a mass hierarchy in a top-down approach.

Graph drawing research has seen significant interest in visualizing graph aesthetics, particularly upward planarity, where all edges point right and up. Although various algorithms exist for identifying upward planar drawings, recognizing whether a directed graph admits an upward planar drawing remains an NP-complete problem. We develop a simpler, more intuitive reduction proving the NP-completeness of upward planarity for bipartite graphs with an unlimited out-degree, as well as a more complex reduction showing $\exists^k$-positivity for bipartite graphs with a limit of two out-degree per node, where $k$ is around 14. These new reductions simplify previously complex reductions and open up the possibility of easier proofs for related variants of upward planarity.

Effectively navigating through memories is crucial for the navigation goals of humans and machines, yet pinpointing the exact memories that are most useful for navigation is complex. Past approaches stored all past experiences in a complete 3D map to facilitate navigation but this method is inefficient due to excessive data and the need for extensive preprocessing. Introducing MemoNav, a novel memory-memory navigation module that selectively accesses only the necessary memories through a memory remembrance process, thus节省ing computational resources and time. The 'remembrance' module trains a small neural network to select the most valuable input memories for navigation, thus creating a two-memory architecture where the selected memories are then used to determine the most probable action to achieve the navigation goal.

The advent of Small Cells in the fourth generation of wireless technology marked a significant turning point, characterized by their low-power, localized range, and modest coverage area. These attributes led to their widespread adoption in the subsequent 4G, 5G, and anticipated 6G wireless generations, primarily driven by the universal need to enhance capacity and extend network reach. As a highly mature technology, Small Cells are poised to play a pivotal role in 6G, where it is expected to be the primary solution for addressing user device connectivity. Consequently, mastering the intricacies of Small Cells is essential for any 6G researcher. This comprehensive article delves into the evolutionary journey of Small Cells, from its inception to its current state, and forecasts future trends. Furthermore, it provides an in-depth analysis of various Small Cell types, their underlying technologies, and potential applications, while also exploring their prospects in 6G, where 6G Small Cells are expected to exhibit even lower power consumption, smaller coverage areas, and deeper penetration capabilities.

In recent years, research in dynamic frameworks has gained attention due to its relevance to real-world problems across various fields, such as engineering and biology. Initially developed for agent networks, this framework has been extended to hypergraphs more recently. This extension allows for more general hyperedge interaction rules, incorporating both even and odd sized edges. Despite being a more comprehensive model, few studies have explored its properties. This work fills that gap by introducing key concepts for dynamic frameworks on hypergraphs, including a novel cover approach for odd edges. Theoretical results show that for 2-coverable graphs, almost all interactions can be resolved. However, for graphs with only odd edges and non-two可 coverable graphs requiring three covers, resolution rates significantly decline. A sparser subclass of hypergraphs is further examined, yielding mixed outcomes based on the size of edges in the cover.

This review examines the equivalence and interconnections of three distinct operator expansion techniques utilized in quantum and statistical field theories. Specifically, the Feynman-Schwinger-Dyson and Legendre transformations are used to formulate field equations, while the Newton-Schrödinger-Legendre transformation generates moving magnon equations. A comprehensive analysis is provided of these methods and their relationships, accompanied by an illustrative example from the $\phi^4$ theory in a $(2+1)$-dimensional space-time. A key observation is that the critical behavior of this system exhibits universal characteristics, independent of whether it's modeled using Feynman-Schwinger-Dyson, Newton-Schrödinger-Legendre, or their variant in magnon language.

In a study of the 8Be + p → ^12C reaction, which is crucial to understanding nuclear reactions at the interface of nuclei and quantum fields, researchers conducted experiments using a TPC and ion detector on the CSNSIR. The researchers observed the resonance at the threshold of the decay of the Hoyle state and measured the direct-decay element of the Hoyle state without the need for medium corrections. The results showed that the direct-decay element of the Hoyle state is -0.122 ± 0.010 (statistics) ± 0.010 (systematics) pm, which agrees with other experimental data within the margins of error. The study also found that the uncertainty in the direct-decay element is smaller than expected and that future research into nuclear direct decay is feasible using a TPC and threshold ion detector.

A comprehensive, one-dimensional fully dynamic brittle fracture model, capable of capturing both oscillatory and tip-dividing instabilities, is presented in this study. The new model incorporates the effects of finite wave propagation speed and inherent material length, represented by the crack surface energy as a function of space and time. The theoretical framework derived from this new framework successfully predicts the onset of these two types of instabilities in materials such as glass, rubber, aluminum, and steel. The conditions for tip-splitting instabilities in the new model match those proposed by the local non-equilibrium thermodynamics and energy balance approaches. However, the theoretical model predicts that tip-splitting instabilities won't occur when the released surface energy doesn't decrease with the crack width. The onset of tip-splitting instabilities, according to the new model, is determined by the balance between the released surface energy and stored elastic energy. The two conditions for tip-splitting and oscillatory instabilities are derived in this study and the model's predictions for crack behavior in different materials are demonstrated in this study.

When transmitting information from an information source through a noisy channel, two main issues arise in communication systems: reliability and efficiency. In this study, we concentrate on channels with limited states transmitted through a noisy channel, where the system's past can influence how the channel behaves. This source-channel separation theorem no longer applies in these scenarios. As a result, knowing the system's past at the sender can help boost communication efficiency. We've developed a new method for efficiently communicating in these situations, where both the sender and receiver have access to their observations and can utilize them to improve performance. This algorithm allows us to find the best possible results as communication progresses and as the message length grows indefinitely, achieving a performance that's nearly as good as the theoretical maximum.

A novel class of superfluids, known as topological superfluids, exhibits unique properties that combine attraction and spin-orbit coupling. In order to study these properties, researchers have utilized the attractive Rashba Hubbard model to investigate the conditions under which topological superfluidity arises. By investigating the ground state of this model, researchers found that a combination of attraction and spin-orbit coupling can give rise to topological superfluids. Furthermore, numerical computations demonstrated that topological superfluidity can occur at relatively weak levels of attraction and spin-orbit coupling. In order to validate these findings, researchers also considered the case of Rashba p-wave superfluidity in a two-dimensional system and demonstrated that topological superfluidity can occur through the formation of a gap in the system's boundary.

This study, SEM-TAB-FACTS, aimed to develop methods for verifying facts and uncovering evidence within tabular data presented in scientific papers. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation on three distinct table types: line items, hierarchical structures and graphs, offering a line-item focused approach, a general framework and a graph-specific method respectively. The competition attracted 14 participating teams, with our evaluation focusing on verifying facts related to COVID-19 and diabetes research papers.

This paper explores the concept of Intricate numbers, emphasizing their relevance in quantum physics. We examine the depth of the quantum state space and within specific multipartite bases, as well as the depth of the image resulting from applying flat and complex linear operators to multipartite states. Our research also delves into the depth of subspaces in quantum physics.

A shortened metric basis of a graph G is the smallest possible set of vertices with the property that for every pair of distinct G-vertices, at least one vertex in the set can differentiate between the vertices' distances to the pair. The concept of shortened metric dimension, which is the size of the smallest shortened metric basis of G, has been investigated in this paper. We establish a relationship between the shortened metric dimension and graph parameters, provide a formula for tree structures, and also consider and discuss specific problems related to trees.

This study introduces two mathematical models to address the movement of groundwater and land surface water level changes in areas with uneven terrain. The first model, based on a time-space formulation of Darcy's law, develops new equations for water flux and transport. The second model, using a mixed formulation of the diffusion equation, develops alternative expressions of water level development. Both models, although mathematically rigorous, provide simplified models compared to traditional approaches in groundwater hydrology. To validate their effectiveness, the models are applied to two real-world cases: the Delaware watershed in the US and the Isle of Wight in the UK. The models, which provide new insights, demonstrate improved computational efficiency of up to 1000 times, making groundwater modeling more feasible.

The effectiveness of an ozone ultraviolet generator in eliminating pollutants in flue gas has been explored. Research indicates that ozone molecules have the capacity to react with nitrogen, forming compounds that scavenge oxygen radicals essential for the breakdown of sulfur compounds. These compounds then recombine to eliminate the remaining radicals and eliminate ozone. In the presence of UV light, ozone molecules break down into stable oxygen, releasing powerful oxygen radicals that can directly attack sulfur compounds and catalyze the oxidation of SO2. The UV light also accelerates the recombination of oxygen radicals, which combine with sulfur compounds to eliminate pollutants in flue gas. The UV light also activates ozone molecules, which combine with water to eliminate pollutants in flue gas. The results of the experiments show that a combined ozone-Ultraviolet unit is more effective at removing SO2 than using ozone or Ultraviolet light alone.

As neuro-morphic technology advances, interest in simulating neural networks is increasing, allowing researchers to design and build future processors. To further this progress, a new tool has been created to simulate entire processor systems, incorporating both traditional and novel processing units. Based on SystemC, a widely accepted hardware design framework, this framework enables simultaneous simulation of multiple processing units. By providing an interface for higher-level software and a flexible interface for hardware designers, the framework helps bridge the gap between software and hardware.

In scenarios such as predicting stock market trends or athlete injuries, binary outcomes are often accompanied by significant uncertainty. Conventional deep learning and even advanced probabilistic models typically ignore this ambiguity to make a single, albeit potentially unreliable, prediction. We introduce a novel approach called Indecision Forests, an extension of decision forests designed to capture and incorporate ambiguity in data. Each node in an Indecision Forest represents a set of possible class labels, which can be learned from argument-based training and ensure are logically consistent. Our method allows us to quantify the confidence in predictions and empowers end-users to incorporate their own doubts into the model. Furthermore, experiments demonstrate that Indecision Forests outperform traditional models in both synthetic real-world applications, providing valuable insights into prediction reliability and enabling users to make more informed decisions.

This paper investigates a minor drawback of the Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) distance, specifically that it requires the computation of an entire alignment, and proposes the PrunedDTW similarity measure to mitigate this issue. PrunedDTW Early Discarding (ED) alignes two time series progressively in a cost-sensitive manner, terminating alignment when it's clear that alignment cost will exceed a predefined threshold. The PrunedDTW distance for two complete time series is then defined as the minimum alignment cost among all possible starting points. The study confirms through experiments that ED significantly reduces computation time, and that the PrunedDTW distance can be efficiently calculated. The findings demonstrate that using the PrunedDTW distance for both filtering and exact search on the entire dataset outperforms traditional methods in terms of search speed while maintaining the recall rate. The code is available on the provided GitHub repository.

This study investigates the efficacy of inquiry-based teaching methods versus traditional detailed feedback in software testing education. Through an educational research study, we compared two approaches: one providing in-depth explanations and the other encouraging student exploration. Our results show that the inquiry-based method outperforms the traditional approach, particularly in fostering student engagement and test case creation. However, individual differences play a role in the outcome, with high-performing students benefiting more from detailed explanations. These findings have significant implications for educators and educational technologists, and a free teaching resource is available to support our teaching approach.

Recent advances in deep neural networks have led to remarkable improvements in many applications, but they have also presented challenges in explaining their decisions. This study explores a new approach called conceptual explanation network (CEN), a hybrid model that integrates the concept learning capabilities of the attribute-value paradigm with the strengths of deep learning. CEN is an innovative method that unites the complementary strengths of existing deep learning techniques and traditional rule-based rule extraction methods, addressing a long-standing dilemma in the field of deep neural networks. CEN is demonstrated to be particularly effective in explaining complex decisions made by state-of-the-art deep neural networks for various tasks, including binary classification, multi-classification, and regression.

Deep graph convolutional neural networks (GCN) have significantly improved various application fields by effectively extracting essential information from graph-structured data. However, GCN's high-level, abstract representation of node features can result in over-smoothing, which negatively impacts performance in tasks like node classification. To counter this issue, our study proposes a novel framework for learning robust node representations through an innovative two-stage process. The first stage involves pre-training GCN layers using a self-supervised method that incorporates both mean-pooling operations and noise injection to generate an accurate global graph image. In the subsequent fine-tuning phase, our self-supervised self-expression model (SSSM) leverages the GCN-predicted global graph image to generate accurate node features, eliminating the need for further graph convolutional operations. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that our SSSM achieves superior performance over existing methods in various benchmark tasks.

Researchers investigated shadow particles interacting with a decaying Z boson in 37.9 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton data collected at 13 TeV by the CMS at the LHC. The study concentrated on events featuring a pair of opposite-charged, high-momentum leptons without associated jets and around a Z boson mass range. The findings matched expectations based on the Standard Model, and researchers determined upper limits on shadow particle interactions at various masses of shadow matter accompanying these events at the 95% confidence level. The produced shadow particles showed a maximum cross-sectional area of 0.42 fb for top quarks, 0.50 fb for Higgs bosons, and 0.54 fb in association with two photons and a scalar boson.

This analysis introduces and investigates $k_\perp$-dependent characteristics that build upon $(g)P\textit{q}D$s but differ from them. It's emphasized that $(g)P\textit{q}D$s can only be understood through lepton-parton scattering processes where the probe's momentum is aligned with the beam's direction. Conversely, the $k_\perp$-dependent characteristics are relevant to parton impact factor theory, enabling the investigation of such factors in various processes, like those involving spin and twist-2/3-dependent parton contributions in events with non-zero transverse momenta for both the probe and the recoil.

A space with a special structure, known as a'space with stockings', features a underlying topological space combined with a space of continuous paths that adhere to specific properties. These properties include compatibility with the original topology through a continuous map and closure under continuous deformations, or'homotopies'. When dealing with spaces that have certain algebraic properties, this structure allows for the creation of algebraic spaces with similar properties, where the limit of these spaces results in spaces with similar properties as well. This properties allows for the construction of spaces with continuous structures by taking colimits of homotopy equivalence classes of maps between algebraic spaces. These spaces with this structure can then be used to construct functors that preserve certain properties as well as universal objects, where the constructed object is equivalent to the space monoidal category of universal objects.

Recent advancements in remote epitaxy technology have enabled the creation of high-performance Heusler single crystals on substrates that were previously incompatible. A recent breakthrough involved growing the inverse spin polarized material Cu2MnSnS4 (CMSTS) on graphene/sapphire substrates using a molecular beam epitaxy process. A detailed analysis of the growth conditions of CMSTS revealed four distinct equilibrium states, each corresponding to a unique epitaxy mechanism. These mechanisms, known as pinhole, distant, and van der Waals epitaxy, as well as a mixed state, can be controlled by adjusting the growth conditions. Furthermore, it was observed that all Heusler single crystals displayed a well-defined (111) epitaxy orientation and exhibited an oxidation-induced surface phase. Our findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on remote epitaxy mechanisms and provide valuable insights for the development of advanced spintronic devices.

In this research, we have created a comprehensive testing framework and confidence intervals for multivariate time series models with robust tails, similar to a t-distribution with finite tails. This interval framework accounts for issues like unequal variances, different correlations between series, and persistent trends. The model incorporates a trend component and a constant correlation structure, while our methods for handling these effects rely on a combination of detrending, pre-whitening, and adjusting critical values for the model's error terms. The results demonstrate that our interval framework effectively captures the behavior of the model's residuals, even in the presence of robust errors.

The initial members of the PEARLS program utilize the powerful capabilities of the JWST to obtain high-resolution spectra of highly magnified regions within EL-Gordo, an object known as ACT-CL J0102-4915, which is located in the past at z=3.33. This program, which uses JWST to study the past, aims to gain a deeper understanding of star and galaxy formation in this object, which is 14 billion light years away. One of the initial targets of this program, which has already received a major upgrade with the NIRCAM G150 mode, reveals a remarkable discovery of a red supergiant star with a temperature of around 3000K and a luminosity of around 100000Lsun. This is the first time such a star has been detected at such a distant location in the universe. Our research also reveals another star, which is located in the same object and has a spectrum similar to that of a red giant star with a temperature of around 4000K and a luminosity around 10000Lsun. This is the first time such a star has been detected with such a high precision. Our research also reveals that the star is located in the same object and is around 100000 parsecs away from us. This is the first time such a star has been detected at such a distant location in the

Internet service providers (ISPs) are tasked with maintaining optimal network functionality, yet they frequently fall short of this goal, as ensuring high-quality service demands substantial effort and resources.  To address a critical industry issue, we examine profit-sharing agreements between content providers and ISPs to incentivize the latter in delivering high-quality service.  We develop a mathematical model to analyze an arbitrary profit-sharing arrangement, identifying conditions that make such agreements beneficial for all parties involved.  To further explore this topic, we model ISPs as competing in a non-cooperative game to determine the equilibrium strategies, equilibrium profit and equilibrium quality of service.  A numerical example demonstrates how our model performs in practice.

In 1954, Segal created a framework in "Hilbert spaces and configurations" that linked observables and system configurations to a set of vectors in a Hilbert space, often interpreted as configurations weighted by the associated measurements. A central question that arose was how to develop this framework into a rigorous form. A central component of Segal's approach was an abstract map from the configurations of a system to the real numbers, representing measurement outcomes. This map needed to preserve symmetry, making it equivariant. In this paper, we show that in the context of systems with group symmetries, Segal's framework forms a universal relationship, or adjunction, in the form of a relationship between two categories. This allows us to create a functor from the configurations to the observations, and a reverse functor from the observations to the configurations, weighted by measurements. This reverse functor assigns to each measurement a space of vectors in the Hilbert space, acting as coefficients in the configuration space. This, in turn, provides a central tool in the quantization of classical systems with symmetries. This paper builds upon earlier work by Rosenberg and the first named author in "The observables and configurations of a classical system" and shows that Rosenberg and Wood's results can be generalized.

The linearized Einstein-scalar equations in the Lorentz gauge exhibit an alpha-parameter scalar-tensor theory background. This is related to the supergravity scalar-tensor field equations through an expansion. The expansion is characterized by an algebraic relation between supergravity and linearized Einstein-scalar equations, along with an expansion parameter that is itself a function of the supergravity fields. This allows for an exact reconstruction of the four-dimensional N=1 supergravity Lagrangian. Furthermore, precise forecasts for the inflationary parameters are calculated.

We establish a evaluation for the foliations at infinity involving hyperbolic metrics derived from quasi-Fuchsian structures that are nearly aligned with a fixed, compact convex cone featuring three-dimensional Euclidean hyperbolic geometry. This important concept was initially introduced and studied by Epstein. Our research accurately determines how these geometries develop as we move away from their common boundary.

This research introduces a novel measure, the Portfolio Yield Dispersion (PYD), to evaluate the level of portfolio heterogeneity. The PYD takes into account the yield differences between portfolio components, providing a single, comprehensive metric that can help assess the impact of portfolio diversity. Empirical results show that portfolios with high dispersion tend to be actively managed, while those with low dispersion often have passive management styles. The PYD also provides valuable insights for fixed-income active managers, as periods of high dispersion are associated with improved forecasting ability and higher yield predictions. The findings suggest that utilizing the second moment of yield curves can help investors capture value in diverse portfolios.

Heart sound detection is a complex task due to the small size of cardiac signals that are often obscured by additive interference and environmental influences. Current approaches relying on artificial neural networks achieve heart sound classification using datasets generated through the combination of clear cardiac signals with background noise, assuming the noise is uniformly distributed. However, this approach is flawed as the noise generation process distorts the underlying signal in a manner inconsistent with real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that simulates noise by modifying a cardiac signal template in a manner that better reflects the characteristics of actual cardiac signals, thereby producing data that more accurately represents cardiac signals found in clinical settings. This approach is then used to train a cardiac sound detector that is robust to the deformation and additive noise. The proposed method is evaluated on clinical data and demonstrates superior performance in comparison to existing methods.

A group of theoretical physicists has created an expanded version of the Standard Model, incorporating the effects of certain new physics interactions in parity-violating optical pumping and L-I-P-O-P-O experiments involving $^{133}$Cs. In addition, the researchers developed an expanded formula that takes into consideration the effects in the "weak bi-dipolar" experiment. They found that their findings match those of earlier calculations in situations where the influence of new physics interactions on bi-dipolar $^{133}$Cs is negligible. In a related development, the physicists published a paper remarking on the limitations of new physics limitations in their work. In response, the physicists have created this note to clarify that the limitations discussed in their original paper are valid under the specific conditions assumed.

A twist of an equivariant homology theory T_*(-) with respect to a finite group G refers to an new theory written as T_*^G(-) with modified coefficients, specifically for G being 2D space groups, T_*^G(-) has equitable homology coefficients, specifically when the theory T_*(-) is equivariant Borel homology for topological G-spectra, with 'equitable' meaning the coefficients are assigned based on isotropy subgroups' conjugacy classes. The twist's existence is demonstrated via the construction of a coefficients spectrum, with the resulting twist's properties expressed through a coefficients spectrum map, with the constructed map's coefficients spectrum given by the equivariant topological K-theory spectrum, with the resulting twist having connections and applications, including an equivalence between the coefficients spectrum and the equivariant topological K-theory spectrum, with the resulting twist having similarities and differences and analogies and distinctions between 'twists on the torus' and 'twists on the sphere'. The equivarient Borel homology theory and its relation to Bredon homology are discussed, with the homeomorphism types of the torus and the sphere being distinguished between in this context.

The fundamental challenge of climate change can be characterized as a collective action problem. A simple, two-player game is employed to illustrate the relationship between atmospheric temperature and the level of greenhouse gases. The game demonstrates how each player benefits initially from reducing their own contribution to greenhouse gases, but eventually reaches a point where their actions lead to a mutual destruction scenario. In this context, the concept of 'Pareto Optimal' refers to outcomes where no individual can be better off, and 'Nash Equilibrium' refers to outcomes where no individual can benefit by changing their own actions alone. Without a partnership, the world's climate would likely deteriorate due to the conflict between these two concepts, and such a decline could have severe long-term consequences. However, through partnership, the values of Pareto Optimality and Nash Equilibrium can be aligned, and such partnerships have potentially positive implications for the concept of 'free will'. Ultimately, the values underlying climate change are rooted in our values as conscious beings, and the solution to climate change may require a reevaluation of our values.

In this paper, we examine the boundedness of a family of sequence operators, which generalize a space-of-type identity operator, between the discrete Hardy space $H^p(\ell^p(\mathbb{Z}^n))$ and BMOA(ℓp(ℤn)) for specific conditions of $p$ and dimension $n$. Additionally, we explore the mapping properties of this family of operators on various function spaces, including the discrete Hardy space $H^p(\ell^p(\mathbb{Z}^n))$ and BMOA(ℓp(ℤn)), as well as the discrete BMOA space $h^p(\ell^p(\mathbb{Z}^n))$ and BMO(ℓp(ℤn)), for specific conditions of $p$ and dimension $n$.

This study explores the presence of ethical bidding strategies, known as second-price rules, in human behavior. We conducted three online auctions to investigate this aspect. The experiments were carried out in environments where participants had no prior knowledge of the second-price rule and were untrained. The results revealed that humans naturally tend to follow the second-price rule in many situations, deviating from it in a limited number of instances. Notably, our findings show that individuals are more likely to adhere to the rule when its existence is acknowledged, and when second-price outcomes can be seen as beneficial for them. Additionally, we discovered that second-order fairness considerations play a limited role in guiding compliance with the rule.

$ f(Q) $, a recently proposed alternative theory, modifies symmetric quadratic gravity. 
We applied this theory to a Bianchi-I cosmos with rotating symmetry, yielding an exact solution where the universe's expansion and isotropic contraction are directly related to its anisotropic contraction and expansion, respectively.
We found that our isotropic solution reduces to the Einstein de Sitter model when a certain theory parameter approaches zero.
We demonstrated that our model avoids the Big Bang, making it a viable alternative to standard $ \Lambda CDM $, YMC, and CCC theories in explaining cosmic acceleration.
We calculated the state of our model during expansion, contraction, and the transition between the two, determining the equations of state and decay rates for both the isotropic and anisotropic fluids.
We investigated the behavior of our model during expansion, finding that it undergoes a phase of decelerated and then accelerated expansion, matching the observed expansion patterns of the universe.
We compared our model to others, including the standard $ \Lambda CDM $, YMC, and CCC models, through dimensionless parameters and found that our model exhibits larger values, indicating greater isotropy.
Our analysis showed that our model naturally explains the large-scale structure of the universe without the need for dark energy or energy, yin-yang conversion, or conformal cyclic cosmology.

Hessenberg varieties, specifically the regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety, have garnered significant interest due to their complex structure and connection to flag manifolds. This work focuses on parameterizing the regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety using geometric vertex partitions, an innovative approach that enables explicit geometric separations based on Gröbner deformations. By associating each partition with a Gröbner system, we achieve variable and function isolations for the resulting deformed variety, thereby extending existing geometric vertex partition techniques. This method not only provides new geometric insights but also computes key invariants, such as Betti numbers, for the regular nilpotent Hessenberg variety.

The surge in neural network applications across various fields has made them a popular tool for creative tasks, particularly in generating artwork, which can be explored by both humans and machines. This competition-driven domain has seen a proliferation of neural art generation methods, outshining traditional computer-generated art in many aspects. This paper delves into the intricacies of the neural art creation process, examining its underlying principles, methods, and challenges, such as the need for aesthetic judgment, and provides a comprehensive survey that can serve as an entry point for researchers and experts in art and vision. Ultimately, the paper envisions a future where neural networks collaborate with human artists, combining the computational prowess of machines with the unique insight of human creativity.

In scenarios involving composite quarks, particularly with a specific arrangement of vector and axial components, calculations involving the Gerasimov-Drell-Hill sum rule and inclusive polarization structure functions have been conducted for both $K$ and $\bar{B}$ mesons. These calculations reveal that the inclusion of sea quark contributions significantly impacts the results, resulting in the GSDH and $g_2$ findings for $K$ and $\bar{B}$ mesons aligning closely with each other, despite expectations of minimal impact from sea quarks. This alignment supports the presence of a particular compositeness model, characterized by a universal behavior of sea quarks and a minimal number of constituents, over alternatives.

This paper presents KQT, an extensive dataset comprising a thousand knowledge seeking queries along with their corresponding responses, derived from the domain of computer science. KQT comprises two distinct parts: KQT-Learn and KQT-Explore. The former is designed for learning tasks, featuring short queries, while KQT-Explore is intended for exploration purposes, characterized by complex queries, diverse formats, and various levels of difficulty. KQT was manually created through careful analysis of research papers in computer science. KQT is a valuable resource for developing and assessing NLP models, particularly those aimed at addressing multi-granularity and long-form query comprehension. KQT is a collaborative project, with further details accessible at kqt-dataset.github.io.

In three-dimensional core-collapse supernova simulations, a core collapse often results in the formation of a pulsating proto-neutron star. This collapse triggers two types of rapid neutrino instabilities: instabilities in positrons and in neutrons. As the accretion shock stalls, it causes convective overturns that transport these instabilities back down, where they persist as long as the accretion shock remains stalled. This coexistence of both instability types in a single convective region creates intricate spatiotemporal patterns, which differ significantly from earlier one-dimensional models and recent three-dimensional calculations that focused primarily on the neutron-driven instability.

ADHD, affecting one in every five children, is a critical condition that has led to the use of MRI scans in recent years for improved diagnosis. The analysis of functional MRI data using machine learning has shown promise in distinguishing between ADHD and control groups in CIP43 and CIP101 challenges. Our research has led to the development of a novel approach called Region Pruning, which identifies and highlights key brain regions for classification. Experiments on the Rosetta Information Network benchmarks demonstrated that our method achieves accurate control/model discrimination, assigning an importance of zero to non-crucial areas. The critical brain areas identified involved regions in the right and left temporal lobes, right central lobe, left frontal lobe, and left parietal lobe. The findings suggest that these regions contain essential information for distinguishing ADHD patients from controls. The reduced number of input features from pruning has also resulted in increased efficiency in the Deep Forest classifier, leading to a faster training time of 10 minutes compared to 2 hours with full data. The success of our method in the two challenges highlights the value of neural network-based feature selection in rs-fMRI data.

A new model is developed to simulate disease spread, taking into account distinct infection periods for susceptible and immune groups. A mathematical analysis is conducted on the model's wellposedness and positive nature. The model's dynamics are examined, including the existence of bounded nontrivial steady states and a unique positive global strong solution. The model is also simulated to study various epidemiological patterns, and the impact of distinct infection periods on disease dynamics is discussed.

This work introduces a new service, an online platform called MadDog, designed to
provide clear explanations of technical jargon and abbreviations within a user's
chosen field of expertise. The MadDog platform offers a customized acronym
解释 service, allowing users to access relevant information about abbreviations
through a straightforward search interface. Users can also contribute to the
database by submitting new jargon and providing their own definitions, which are
validated by existing database contributors. Furthermore, the MadDog platform
enables users to upload existing jargon databases for free, providing valuable
resources for other users to access.

Our research reveals that magnetic interference can significantly impact the flow of heat in quantum Hall junctions, which in turn affects their ability to convert heat into electricity. By adjusting the magnetic field and voltage applied, we found that this heat-related behavior can be controlled and used to create structures that direct heat in one direction. This effect was best when influenced by two levels of heat and varied with temperature. This study demonstrates that delicate changes in a material's response to heat can be triggered by external factors, which may enable the development of unique, highly efficient heat-based electronic devices.

Recent advancements in DNA-based storage technology have demonstrated high data density and efficient parallel processing, but its adoption is hindered by difficulties in managing data structurally and updating information. Traditional DNA storage systems, which use flat hierarchies and static information update policies, lead to frequent and costly reencoding. To address these limitations, a new management system has been developed, incorporating information update policies and efficient hierarchical structures to reduce reencoding costs. This novel DNA storage management system, which takes into account real-world constraints, also proposes using the B-Tree data structure to facilitate faster and more cost-effective data updates. Our research demonstrates that this reencoding-assisted management system achieves a 10x reduction in reencoding costs, as well as a 100x and 1000x improvement in efficiency for moderate and large-scale datasets, respectively, compared to traditional DNA storage policies.

Algebraic node-based models for topological insulators date back to the late 90s, featuring simple global expressions for partial Hamiltonians with fixed odd parity under time reversal. These models have extensive applications in various condensed matter systems, including Weyl semimetals, driven quantum systems, and, notably, topological photonics thanks to the development of nanoassemblies. We review the principles of nanoassemblies and provide examples of nodal surface implementations, discussing their stabilization by symmetry and spontaneous breakdown.

Previous research has utilized analytical methods to generate theoretical velocity estimates for pacemaker-induced waves in certain isotropic systems. This study extends such estimates to conditions with directional properties by formulating the generalized FitzHugh-Nagumo equations. Corresponding theoretical estimates are derived and compared with computational simulations for both pacemaker-generated and heterogeneous ring cases.

Approximating the von Neumann entropy of a quantum state is a fundamental task in both theoretical and practical applications. In this study, we analyze the complexity of this approximation problem, considering the state is provided either as black-box subroutines or a polynomial number of copies. For the black-box model, our method achieves an entropy approximation up to additive $\epsilon \log(1/\delta)$ using only $O(\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\epsilon^2}\log^4 n)$ calls, marking an improvement over previous work. For a specific class of states, we find a more efficient solution requiring $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2}\log^4 n)$ calls. In the copy model, our method finds a state property that can be estimated using $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2}\log n$ copies. Furthermore, we explore a line of reasoning to compute the trace distance between purifications of unknown states using a line of reasoning from quantum property testing, yielding an upper bound.

The increasing reliance on artificial intelligence (AI) in data-driven industries is driven by the need for intelligent systems capable of processing vast amounts of data. However, the decision to utilize AI technology involves complex technical considerations, particularly in workflow optimization and infrastructure management. Key issues such as AI model development, feature engineering, and inference require careful planning and efficient use of computational resources. The choice between on-premise and cloud-based solutions has significant implications for cost, scalability, and operational flexibility. Cloud-based AI services offer enhanced accessibility and resource elasticity, but also present challenges related to data security, compliance, and vendor lock-in. Ultimately, the successful adoption of AI technology depends on addressing these technical complexities and making informed decisions that balance innovation with practical constraints.

This study proposes an innovative, semi-supervised approach for automatically identifying ICD diagnosis codes from clinical text using NLP. By leveraging a small set of labeled data and an extensive corpus of unlabelled data, this method capitalizes on word embeddings to improve its performance. Compared to fully supervised models trained on clinical text and paired ICD codes, the semi-supervised approach demonstrates considerable improvements in accuracy, particularly for tasks involving challenging Aesop and ICD-9 vocabularies. By integrating unsupervised learning with supervised tasks, this method offers an efficient and precise solution for guiding healthcare professionals in selecting ICD codes.

Consider a monomial ideal $I$ in a polynomial ring $S$, with the property that local cohomology modules $H^{i}_{\mathfrak{m}}(I^{k}_{j})$ are finitely generated for all non-negative integers $i$ and a fixed integer $k$ where $i$ is less than or equal to the codimension of $I$ and $j$ is a positive integer. The codegrees of the minimal generators of $I_{j}$, when taken for each degree $d$, form a set which is known to be minimal. In the context of nearly Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideals, a characterization is provided that involves these codegree sets, and as an example, a specific nearly Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideal is constructed with the help of a monomial curve in the polynomial ring $S$.

A breakthrough in machine learning and data analysis is anticipated through the utilization of quantum devices, taking advantage of the capabilities of quantum systems. Nevertheless, the quantum learning model is largely confined by the lack of access to labeled data required for supervised learning tasks. To overcome this obstacle, we have devised an unmonitored quantum learning model capable of functioning in the absence of labeled data. The model is designed to be compatible with various quantum devices and can be easily adapted to different types of quantum systems. We have also developed a monitored version of the model that leverages data from labeled and unlabeled sets. In addition, we have implemented the model on a superconducting quantum processor and obtained promising results, showcasing its effectiveness in classifying data and solving the XOR problem.

The Kilometre Network for Visual Telescopes (KMTNet) is conducting a continuous survey of the Southern Sky to find celestial objects that suddenly change brightness. In 2018, the KMTNet team thoroughly observed eight distinct regions of the sky using the telescope at Siding Spring Observatory. They discovered 1,073 new objects in these areas, out of a total of 10,203 examined, which represented a rate of three discoveries for every hundred objects found. This discovery rate was consistent across all eight regions of the sky, with no differences in the types of objects found. A total of 70% of these new objects were microlensing events, 27% were comets, and the remaining 2% were other types of objects. About 17% of the events that fit the pattern of a lensing object passing in front of another object had what appeared to be multiple sources, and about half of the objects that moved across the sky in the expected direction for such events showed signs of being blocked or obscured.

Two main types of inverse issues exist: those that can be resolved by directly comparing data and simulations, and those that require finding the best-match between data and simulations, typically requiring an optimization process. In this research, an efficient method for determining shadows is presented, which facilitates the resolution of challenging simulation-based inverse problems by leveraging the previously established path-tracing technique. The proposed method, based on back-propagation of signals, is introduced and shown to be differentiable, thus enabling the utilization of modern gradient-based optimization methods. The research also features practical applications, including the reconstruction of a turbulent jet and box-shaped objects from partial data.

Stochastic origin-destination demand estimation is crucial for real-time traffic management and transportation network monitoring. Traditional methods focus on deterministic demand estimation using aggregate traffic data, while our work addresses stochastic demand estimation using a multi-class traffic flow model based on cell transmission theory. By applying maximum a posteriori (MAP) and iterative expected responsibility maximization (IERM) algorithms, we achieve demand estimation with an average mean absolute error of 0.00000028 and 0.00000002, respectively. Furthermore, our method enables real-time demand estimation with acceptable computation times, thus facilitating stochastic traffic management.

The oscillations of multiple coupled non-linear oscillators, each comprising a distinct pair of variables, exhibit multiple degrees of freedom that are crucial for understanding their behavior. Typically, research has focused on systems with identical or conjugate components, where phase-based descriptions effectively capture their dynamics. However, we investigate the broader applicability of phase-based descriptions to more complex systems, including those with mixed and anisotropic components, using the example of an anisotropic Kummer array. Our results reveal the existence of unique fixed points and describe the conditions under which phase-based descriptions are coherent and apply. Additionally, we demonstrate the presence of both desynchronized and synchronized states within these conditions, as well as the emergence of low-dimensional attractors resulting from the coupling. Our findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of more complex and practically relevant systems, such as those with anisotropic Kerr microresonators, Kerr waveguide arrays, and optical microtoroid arrays.

The probability distribution of Aldous and Broder and Wilson's algorithm both result in uniform spanning trees. The joint distribution of their algorithms' outputs is analyzed in this article. First, the article calculates the probability that both algorithms generate the same spanning tree. Next, the differences between the two algorithms are explored. The discovered disparities are substantial; for instance, the Central Limit Theorem's applicability to path lengths is affected differently. In contrast, Wilson's algorithm exhibits a lack of influence over the start node, while theoretical models suggest that tree structure can be used to find hidden categories. Furthermore, the article's findings can be used to create a two-phase algorithm, which generates a uniform spanning tree. In this algorithm, a primary random walk is created to capture essential information, and the actual algorithm is chosen based on these findings, combining the strengths of both methods.

A dataset known as musicTM is presented, designed to bring together sheet music, lyrics, and the underlying music audio. This dataset paves the way for developing unified models capable of processing sheet music, lyrics, and music audio simultaneously, ultimately enabling a wide range of applications in music-related tasks. Initially, three distinct sub-datasets focusing on individual components (sheet music, lyrics, and music audio) are created to promote research in each respective area. Subsequently, a combined dataset integrating all sub-components is developed to demonstrate the feasibility of unified representation learning. The dataset musicTM contains a total of 17,073 individual music pieces, featuring high-quality sheet music scanned from original scores, corresponding text metadata including titles, composers, and lyrics, and high-fidelity music audio recordings. Notably, musicTM stands out as the largest and most comprehensive dataset available for unified music representation.

Natural language processing enables the integration of unstructured text and graphical images, which can be analyzed using knowledge graphs like Ontodia and Wikidata. By combining text embeddings, we can enhance query capabilities and data analysis, ultimately enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the linked data. This work demonstrates the capabilities of text embeddings by using a knowledge graph based on natural language processing. We present a case study using Ontodia and Wikidata to show how text embeddings can facilitate both automated and human-assisted examination of the linked data. By using a language model, we can perform automatic information retrieval and, in conjunction with an intelligent user interface, propose relevant entities. Ultimately, this leads to a more efficient and effective examination of the linked data.

The influence of dispersion changes on soliton stability in one-dimensional optical systems with intense light is investigated. An intensity-dependent optical dispersion model is proposed, and its effect on dark soliton stability in the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation is examined. It is found that increasing dispersion intensity dependence can have a stabilizing effect on dark solitons, and that a new type of dark soliton with a curved profile can emerge.

We are introducing a novel framework, called Lotse, which allows for the creation of interactive and customizable assistance systems in visual analytics. By leveraging functional programming, the framework facilitates the development of flexible and maintainable models. We will discuss our design principles, a core framework for assistance, and a library of models and strategies.
